speaker: Doctor
text: I see you are experiencing persistent vomiting and chest pain. To help me understand what is going on, can you describe the nature of the chest pain—is it sharp, dull, or pressure-like—and does it radiate to your arm or jaw?

speaker: Patient
text: 51-year-old male. The patient presents to the emergency department with persistent, forceful vomiting after consuming a significant amount of alcohol. His medical history includes recent treatment for Lyme disease with doxycycline. Recently, after a prolonged episode of retching, the patient starts to choke and cough forcefully, experiencing chest pain. The patient appears unable to communicate effectively at this point.

speaker: Doctor
text: I have noted the patient's history of alcohol-induced vomiting and subsequent chest pain with choking, which raises concern for a possible esophageal rupture. Since the patient is currently unable to communicate, I will proceed with diagnostic imaging to confirm the extent of the injury. REQUEST TEST: Chest_X-Ray

speaker: Doctor
text: The chest X-ray shows free mediastinal air, which strongly suggests a perforation of the esophagus. To confirm the location and severity of the tear, I need to visualize the esophagus directly. REQUEST TEST: Contrast_Esophagram

speaker: Doctor
text: A normal contrast esophagram is unexpected given the mediastinal air, so I need to rule out other causes or confirm the leak with a more sensitive modality. REQUEST TEST: CT_Chest_with_contrast

speaker: Doctor
text: The CT scan confirms contrast extravasation from the distal esophagus into the mediastinum, which definitively diagnoses the injury. Given the history of forceful vomiting followed by chest pain and these imaging findings, the clinical picture is classic for Boerhaave syndrome. DIAGNOSIS READY: Boerhaave syndrome
